tier_reason: First-party Google Benchmark output in the README (Apple M3 Pro) with public harness code (tools/YuvBenchmarkMain.cpp, tools/bench/YuvBenchmark10.cpp, tools/bench/YuvSupport.cpp, tools/bench/YuvBenchmarkNV.cpp), but no compiler, no flags for the published run, no test-image size and an unversioned prebuilt libyuv.a, so not A; no independent measurement, so not B.

corrections.workload: Google Benchmark timings (one conversion per iteration; the YCbCr paths are single-threaded, threading is only used by FastGaussian) of 8-bit and 10-bit YCbCr 4:4:4/4:2:2/4:2:0 to RGBA decode, RGBA8 to YCbCr 4:2:0/4:2:2 encode, NV12/NV21 to RGBA decode, and RGBA premultiply/unpremultiply, sparkyuv vs libyuv (I444/I422/I420ToABGR, I410/I210/I010ToARGBMatrix, NV12/NV21 conversions, ARGBAttenuate/ARGBUnattenuate) on one JPEG test image (filirovska.jpeg, not in the repo, dimensions not stated) expanded to opaque RGBA; libyuv is linked from a prebuilt libyuv.a of unstated version and build flags.
corrections.claimed_speedup: README, Apple M3 Pro, ns per call: 10-bit YCbCr 4:2:0 decode 569,507 vs libyuv 1,090,866 (1.92x); 10-bit 4:2:2 552,089 vs 1,092,268 (1.98x); 10-bit 4:4:4 620,223 vs 1,314,001 (2.12x). 8-bit decode 4:2:2 346,422 vs 458,754 (1.32x); 4:2:0 347,903 vs 458,823 (1.32x); 4:4:4 332,122 vs 365,939 (1.10x); NV21 394,745 vs 407,932; NV12 386,739 vs 387,258 (tie). Unpremultiply 895,136 vs 1,382,779 (1.54x). Slower than libyuv: RGBA8 to YCbCr420 543,371 vs 270,961 (libyuv 2.0x faster); RGBA8 to YCbCr422 552,492 vs 402,977 (libyuv 1.37x faster); premultiply 259,198 vs 213,810 (libyuv 1.21x faster). All ratios derived from page data. In the 10-bit rows sparkyuv writes 10-bit RGBA (16 bits per channel) while libyuv's *ToARGBMatrix writes 8-bit ARGB, so the two sides produce different outputs.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the published run; the repository CMakeLists.txt builds C++20, adds -O3 to Release builds on non-MSVC compilers and uses Highway static dispatch on Apple (HWY_COMPILE_ONLY_STATIC). Compiler and libyuv build flags unknown.
corrections.caveats: Mixed result: the README says 8-bit decode is 'very close to libyuv', faster only on arm64 NEON and 'should be considered same' elsewhere, and libyuv is faster at 8-bit YCbCr encode (2.0x at 4:2:0, 1.37x at 4:2:2) and premultiply. The 10-bit wins compare different outputs (sparkyuv 10-bit RGBA in 16-bit storage vs libyuv 8-bit ARGB). Only arm64 numbers; no x86 results. Test image is not in the repo and its size is not stated; premultiply/unpremultiply run on fully opaque pixels from an RGB JPEG. libyuv comes from a prebuilt libyuv.a of unknown version and flags. Repo archived by owner 10 Feb 2025; last commit 14 Jul 2024. Licence files: LICENSE.md (Apache-2.0) and LICENSE-BSD.md (BSD-3-Clause, same author); source headers cite Apache-2.0.

notes: Every number in the record matches the README benchmark block; I added the 10-bit 4:4:4/4:2:2, 8-bit 4:2:0, NV21 and RGBA8-to-YCbCr422 rows and labelled ratios as derived. The headline 10-bit 1.9-2.1x gains are not like-for-like (10-bit RGBA output vs libyuv's 8-bit ARGB output), which the enricher should keep visible. Metadata (9 stars, archived 2025-02-10, last commit 2024-07-14) checked on github.com.

tier_reason: First-party README tables against libyuv and Apple Accelerate on Apple M1 and i7-8700B; the linked harness (xxImGui experimental branch) no longer contains any YUV benchmark code that I could find, and no compiler, flags, libyuv version or image size are given.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README, microseconds, xxYUV vs libyuv: i7-8700B AVX2 encode YU12/YV12 31 vs 48, NV12/NV21 33 vs 39; decode YU12/YV12 46 vs 60, NV12/NV21 39 vs 54. Apple M1 NEON encode 37 vs 48 and 38 vs 49; decode 38 vs 122 and 42 vs 89. That is 1.2-1.55x on encode and 1.3x (AVX2) to 3.2x (M1 NEON) on decode (derived from page data). xxYUV also beats Accelerate on every reported row (M1 NEON decode 38 vs 62, i7 AVX2 encode 31 vs 83). On M1 x86 builds (SSSE3) encode is 134 vs libyuv 146.
corrections.caveats: First-party, no compiler or flags, no libyuv version, image size not stated. The README points to https://github.com/metarutaiga/xxImGui/tree/experimental as the benchmark environment, but at that branch's head (repository archived 17 Aug 2025) the plugin directory holds only sample and validator plugins with no YUV code, and its commits up to Oct 2021 do not mention YUV or libyuv, so the harness cannot be inspected. Conversions use 8-bit fixed-point BT.709 coefficients (Y scaled by 256, vqdmulh/mulhi multiplies); output accuracy versus libyuv is not reported and the libyuv matrix used is unknown. Last commit 20 Oct 2021.

notes: All README numbers match the record. Tier stays C: the benchmark harness the README links to is not findable at the xxImGui experimental head, so I could not read the measured code. The record's 'SSSE3 and SSE2 under Rosetta' for the M1 table is an inference (the README just lists x86 SIMD rows under Apple M1).

tier_reason: First-party README tables (added 22 Sep 2018, z.lib 2.8) against FFmpeg 4.0.2 filters on two named Intel CPUs; the FFmpeg filter strings are given, but no compiler, flags, thread count, frame content or the zimg command line, so not A, and no independent measurement, so not B.

corrections.baseline: FFmpeg 4.0.2 filters (README column label 'swscale 4.0.2'): the swscale scale filter for the Lanczos resize and the libavfilter colorspace filter for the BT.709 to BT.2020 conversion
corrections.workload: Time in ms to resize an FHD frame to UHD with the Lanczos filter (FFmpeg side: scale=3840:2160:sws_flags=lanczos+accurate_rnd:sws_dither=none), and to convert an FHD frame from BT.709 YUV to BT.2020 (FFmpeg side: the colorspace filter, colorspace=all=bt2020:iall=bt709:format=yuv420p10, which is libavfilter's vf_colorspace rather than swscale).
corrections.caveats: README numbers only, added in commit 'Add performance information to README.md' on 22 Sep 2018 with z.lib 2.8 and FFmpeg 4.0.2, so they are about eight years old and swscale has been reworked since. zimg ships its own timing tools (src/testapp resizeapp.cpp and colorspaceapp.cpp take a --times benchmark-cycles option), but the README gives no command lines, compiler, flags, thread count or frame content for either side. The second row's baseline is FFmpeg's colorspace filter, not swscale. A Doom9 forum thread (blocked here; search snippet only, poster and date unknown) reports mixed results: zimg faster for Lanczos upscaling, swscale faster for YUV420P8 to RGB24. Licence is WTFPL v2 (graphengine submodule also WTFPL): permissive and public-domain-equivalent but not OSI-approved; no patent grant.

notes: README numbers match the record exactly (7.7 vs 15.2, 10.8 vs 22.2, 8.3 vs 17.5, 11.5 vs 25.6 ms). I kept usability copyable on the reading that WTFPL is a public-domain-equivalent grant like CC0; under a strict OSI-only reading it would be reference, so the orchestrator may want to rule on WTFPL once.
